elements.name: Client-Server
elements.what: System organized as clients that request services from one or more server components over a connector.
elements.problem: Centralize shared data/computation while letting many independent consumers access it; separates presentation/consumption from provision.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Perspectives on an Emerging Discipline - Shaw & Garlan (1996)

elements.name: N-Tier Architecture
elements.what: System partitioned into physically separable tiers (presentation, domain/logic, data) each deployable on its own node class.
elements.problem: Scale and evolve presentation, business logic, and storage independently; confine technology choices and load per tier.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002), ch.1 Layering

elements.name: Monolithic Architecture
elements.what: The whole application is built and deployed as a single deployable unit.
elements.problem: Simplicity of development, testing, and deployment for one team/one unit; the named baseline against which service decomposition trades off.
elements.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - Monolithic Architecture - Richardson (living)

elements.name: Modular Monolith
elements.what: Single deployable unit whose interior is decomposed into strictly encapsulated modules with enforced boundaries.
elements.problem: Keep monolith deployment simplicity while getting service-like boundary discipline; a stepping stone to (or alternative to) microservices.
elements.named_in: Monolith to Microservices - Newman (2019)

elements.name: Microservices
elements.what: Suite of small, independently deployable services, each owning its data, communicating over lightweight network mechanisms, organized around business capabilities.
elements.problem: Independent deployability, team autonomy, and heterogeneous technology per service; trades operational and distribution complexity for decoupling.
elements.named_in: Microservices - Lewis & Fowler (martinfowler.com, 2014)

elements.name: Service-Oriented Architecture
elements.what: Enterprise organized as coarse-grained reusable business/enterprise services coordinated through a mediating integration layer (often an ESB/orchestrator).
elements.problem: Enterprise-wide reuse of business functions across applications; centralizes integration and workflow at the cost of coupling to the mediator.
elements.named_in: Fundamentals of Software Architecture - Richards & Ford (2020)

elements.name: Service-Based Architecture
elements.what: Small number of coarse-grained, separately deployed domain services sharing a single database, typically fronted by one UI.
elements.problem: Pragmatic middle ground between monolith and microservices: partial independent deployability without distributed-data complexity.
elements.named_in: Fundamentals of Software Architecture - Richards & Ford (2020)

elements.name: Event-Driven Architecture
elements.what: System of decoupled components that produce and react to asynchronously delivered events rather than making direct requests.
elements.problem: High decoupling, elasticity, and responsiveness for workflows that are naturally reactive; trades away easy end-to-end reasoning and transactional simplicity.
elements.named_in: Fundamentals of Software Architecture - Richards & Ford (2020)

elements.name: Space-Based Architecture
elements.what: Processing units with replicated in-memory data grids, synchronized asynchronously to persistent storage, so the database is out of the request path.
elements.problem: Extreme/variable concurrency where the database is the bottleneck; achieves elastic scale by removing the central data store from the hot path.
elements.named_in: Fundamentals of Software Architecture - Richards & Ford (2020)

elements.name: Peer-to-Peer
elements.what: Symmetric nodes acting as both clients and servers, cooperating without a central coordinator.
elements.problem: Decentralized resource sharing, resilience to single-node failure, and scale without central infrastructure.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

elements.name: SEDA (Staged Event-Driven Architecture)
elements.what: Service structured as a network of event-driven stages connected by explicit queues, each stage with its own thread pool and admission control.
elements.problem: Well-conditioned behavior under massive load: per-stage queues give backpressure points and prevent overcommit that thread-per-request designs suffer.
elements.named_in: SEDA: An Architecture for Well-Conditioned, Scalable Internet Services - Welsh, Culler & Brewer (SOSP 2001)

elements.name: Shared-Nothing Architecture
elements.what: Nodes own disjoint partitions of data and memory and coordinate only by messages; no shared disk or shared memory.
elements.problem: Horizontal scalability without contention on shared resources; each node scales independently, at the price of cross-partition coordination.
elements.named_in: The Case for Shared Nothing - Stonebraker (1986)

elements.name: MapReduce
elements.what: Batch computation structured as a parallel map phase over partitioned input, a shuffle, and a reduce phase, scheduled across a cluster by a framework.
elements.problem: Run large-scale data processing on commodity clusters while the framework handles partitioning, scheduling, and fault recovery.
elements.named_in: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters - Dean & Ghemawat (OSDI 2004)

elements.name: Lambda Architecture
elements.what: Data system split into a batch layer (immutable master dataset, recomputed views), a speed layer (incremental real-time views), and a serving layer merging both.
elements.problem: Combine the accuracy/robustness of batch recomputation with low-latency access to recent data.
elements.named_in: Big Data: Principles and best practices of scalable realtime data systems - Marz & Warren (2015)

elements.name: Kappa Architecture
elements.what: Everything is a stream: a single stream-processing pipeline over a replayable log serves both real-time and reprocessing needs, eliminating the separate batch layer.
elements.problem: Avoid maintaining dual batch/speed code paths of the lambda architecture; reprocessing is replaying the log through the same pipeline.
elements.named_in: Questioning the Lambda Architecture - Kreps (O'Reilly Radar, 2014)

elements.name: Serverless / Function-as-a-Service
elements.what: Application logic deployed as provider-managed, event-triggered ephemeral functions (plus managed backend services), with no server capacity owned by the team.
elements.problem: Eliminate server provisioning and idle cost; scale-to-zero and per-invocation billing, traded against cold starts, execution limits, and provider coupling.
elements.named_in: Serverless Architectures - Roberts (martinfowler.com, 2016)

elements.name: Publish-Subscribe (system topology)
elements.what: System-scale interaction style where producers publish events to an intermediary and consumers subscribe by topic/content, with no mutual knowledge.
elements.problem: Space, time, and synchronization decoupling among many communicating systems; adding consumers requires no producer change.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: in-process pub-sub is the design realm's observer/event-aggregator/publish-subscribe-channel; this entry is the cross-system topology sense (per Phase 1 parked decision).

elements.name: Micro Frontends
elements.what: Frontend decomposed into independently built and deployed UI fragments owned end-to-end by the teams owning the corresponding backend services.
elements.problem: Extend microservice-style team autonomy through the UI layer instead of funneling all teams through one frontend monolith.
elements.named_in: Micro Frontends - Jackson (martinfowler.com, 2019)

elements.name: Cell-Based Architecture
elements.what: Workload deployed as multiple isolated, self-sufficient instances (cells), each serving a partition of requests, with a thin router directing traffic to cells.
elements.problem: Reduce blast radius: a failure or bad deployment is contained to one cell's share of traffic; fault-isolation bulkheads at workload level.
elements.named_in: Reducing the Scope of Impact with Cell-Based Architecture - AWS Well-Architected (2023)

elements.name: Data Mesh
elements.what: Analytical data architecture decentralized into domain-owned data products with self-serve platform and federated governance, instead of one central lake/warehouse.
elements.problem: Central data teams become bottlenecks and lose domain context at scale; aligns data ownership with domain (bounded-context) boundaries.
elements.named_in: How to Move Beyond a Monolithic Data Lake to a Distributed Data Mesh - Dehghani (martinfowler.com, 2019)
elements.borderline: Organizational/socio-technical as much as structural; kept because it is an established named reference structure and a bridge endpoint for bounded-context-aligned data elements.

elements.name: Model-View-Controller
elements.what: Interactive application divided into a model (state and logic), views (presentation), and controllers (input handling), with change propagation from model to views.
elements.problem: Keep multiple presentations consistent with shared state while allowing UI to change independently of core logic.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1 - Buschmann et al. (1996); original: Reenskaug (Xerox PARC, 1979)

elements.name: Model-View-Presenter
elements.what: UI structure where a presenter mediates all interaction between a (possibly passive) view and the model, absorbing presentation logic.
elements.problem: Make GUI logic testable and views thin by moving decision logic out of widgets into a mediating presenter.
elements.named_in: MVP: Model-View-Presenter - Potel (Taligent, 1996)

elements.name: Model-View-ViewModel
elements.what: UI structure where a view binds declaratively (data binding) to a view-model exposing view-shaped state and commands over the model.
elements.problem: Exploit data-binding frameworks so views need no imperative glue code and presentation state is testable without the UI toolkit.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Model/View/ViewModel pattern - Gossman (Microsoft blog, 2005)

elements.name: Presentation Model
elements.what: A self-contained class holding all view state and behavior, which the view synchronizes with; the toolkit-independent predecessor of MVVM.
elements.problem: Pull view state and logic out of widgets into a testable object when the toolkit lacks data binding.
elements.named_in: Further Enterprise Application Architecture development - Fowler (eaaDev, 2004)

elements.name: Flux
elements.what: App structure with a strict one-way cycle: views dispatch actions, a dispatcher routes them to stores, stores update and re-render views.
elements.problem: Tame cascading, hard-to-trace two-way binding updates in complex UIs by forcing all state change through one auditable direction.
elements.named_in: Flux: In-Depth Overview - Facebook (2014)

elements.name: The Elm Architecture
elements.what: App structured as an immutable model, a pure update function folding messages into the model, and a pure view function rendering it.
elements.problem: Make whole-app state transitions pure, replayable, and exhaustively type-checked; the functional refinement of unidirectional data flow.
elements.named_in: The Elm Architecture - Czaplicki (Official Elm Guide, living)

elements.name: Hexagonal Architecture
elements.what: Application core exposes technology-neutral ports; adapters translate between each external actor (UI, DB, tests, other systems) and the ports.
elements.problem: Let the application be driven equally by users, programs, or tests, and keep infrastructure swappable; kills business-logic leakage into UI and DB code.
elements.named_in: Hexagonal Architecture - Cockburn (alistair.cockburn.us, 2005)

elements.name: Clean Architecture
elements.what: Concentric layers (entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks) with all source dependencies pointing inward toward policy.
elements.problem: Keep business rules independent of frameworks, UI, and databases so they outlive delivery mechanisms; generalizes hexagonal/onion into one dependency discipline.
elements.named_in: Clean Architecture - Martin (2017)

elements.name: Bounded Context
elements.what: An explicit boundary within which a domain model and its ubiquitous language apply consistently; large systems are partitioned into several.
elements.problem: One unified enterprise model fails at scale; explicit context boundaries prevent model corruption and define natural service/ownership seams.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design - Evans (2003)

elements.name: Context Map
elements.what: A documented map of the system's bounded contexts and the relationship type at each seam (partnership, customer-supplier, conformist, ACL, ...).
elements.problem: Teams need a shared, honest picture of model boundaries and inter-context translation obligations to coordinate integration.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design - Evans (2003)

elements.name: Anti-Corruption Layer
elements.what: An isolating translation layer between two bounded contexts (typically new model and legacy/external system) that converts between the two models.
elements.problem: Integrate with a system whose model you must not absorb; keeps the foreign model from leaking into and corrupting your own.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design - Evans (2003)

elements.name: API Gateway
elements.what: Single entry point that routes, composes, and adapts client requests to backend services, and absorbs cross-cutting edge concerns (auth, TLS, rate limits).
elements.problem: Clients should not know service decomposition or make chatty cross-service calls; edge concerns should not be re-implemented per service.
elements.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - API Gateway - Richardson (living)

elements.name: Backends for Frontends
elements.what: One purpose-built edge/API backend per frontend type (mobile, web, ...), each owned by the corresponding frontend team.
elements.problem: A single general-purpose gateway becomes a contended, lowest-common-denominator bottleneck when client types have divergent needs.
elements.named_in: Backends For Frontends - Newman (samnewman.io, 2015)

elements.name: Service Mesh
elements.what: Dedicated infrastructure layer of per-service proxies (data plane) plus a control plane that transparently handles inter-service traffic: routing, retries, mTLS, telemetry.
elements.problem: Move reliability and security of service-to-service communication out of every application's code into uniform, operable infrastructure.
elements.named_in: What's a service mesh? And why do I need one? - Morgan (Buoyant, 2017)

elements.name: Sidecar
elements.what: A helper process/container co-deployed with an application instance, sharing its lifecycle and local resources to extend it (proxying, logging, config).
elements.problem: Add cross-cutting capabilities to heterogeneous services without changing their code or language; per-instance co-location keeps latency and fate-sharing local.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Container-based Distributed Systems - Burns & Oppenheimer (HotCloud 2016)

elements.name: Ambassador
elements.what: A sidecar variant that proxies the application's outbound connections to the outside world, hiding discovery, sharding, or protocol detail.
elements.problem: Let a component talk to remote dependencies as if local and unsharded; the ambassador absorbs routing/resilience client logic.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Container-based Distributed Systems - Burns & Oppenheimer (HotCloud 2016)

elements.name: Adapter (container)
elements.what: A sidecar variant that presents a standardized interface (e.g., uniform metrics/log format) over a heterogeneous application to the rest of the system.
elements.problem: Uniform monitoring/management across services built differently, without modifying each service.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Container-based Distributed Systems - Burns & Oppenheimer (HotCloud 2016)
elements.borderline: Shares the GoF Adapter name; kept separate: this is a deployment-unit structure, not an object-interface mechanism.

elements.name: Strangler Fig
elements.what: Incrementally build the new system around the edges of the old, intercepting and redirecting functionality until the legacy system is fully displaced.
elements.problem: Big-bang rewrites fail; this gives continuously shippable migration with reversible steps and a shrinking legacy core.
elements.named_in: StranglerFigApplication - Fowler (bliki, 2004)

elements.name: Saga
elements.what: A multi-step business transaction implemented as a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to semantically undo it on failure.
elements.problem: Atomic distributed transactions (2PC) are unavailable or too coupling across services; sagas trade isolation for availability with explicit compensation.
elements.named_in: Sagas - Garcia-Molina & Salem (SIGMOD 1987)

elements.name: Orchestration
elements.what: A central coordinator component explicitly directs the steps of a multi-service workflow, tracking state and invoking each participant.
elements.problem: Complex workflows need visible state, ordering, and error handling in one place; trades a coordination hub (and its coupling) for traceability.
elements.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - Saga (orchestration variant) - Richardson (living)

elements.name: Choreography
elements.what: Multi-service workflows emerge from services publishing and reacting to each other's events, with no central coordinator.
elements.problem: Avoid a coordination bottleneck and keep services autonomous; trades away a single place to see and control workflow state.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Choreography - Azure Architecture Center (living)

elements.name: Transactional Outbox
elements.what: Service writes outgoing messages into an outbox table within the local database transaction; a relay publishes them to the broker afterwards.
elements.problem: Atomically update state and publish an event without distributed transactions across a database and a message broker.
elements.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - Transactional Outbox - Richardson (living)

elements.name: CQRS
elements.what: The system's write model (commands) and read model (queries) are separated into distinct models, often with distinct stores kept in sync asynchronously.
elements.problem: Read and write workloads have divergent shapes and scale; one canonical model serves both poorly. Costs eventual consistency between models.
elements.named_in: CQRS Documents - Young (2010); also CQRS - Fowler (bliki, 2011)

elements.name: Event Sourcing (architecture style)
elements.what: System-level persistence strategy where the event log is the source of truth for whole services and downstream projections/read models are derived from it.
elements.problem: Full audit/history, temporal queries, and rebuildable projections across a system; couples consumers to event schemas over time.
elements.named_in: Event Sourcing - Fowler (eaaDev, 2005)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm's event-sourcing entry is the in-component persist-as-events mechanism; this entry is the system-level style built on it.

elements.name: Event-Carried State Transfer
elements.what: Events carry the full changed state so consumers maintain local replicas and need not call back to the source system.
elements.problem: Decouple availability and latency of consumers from the source system; trades data duplication and eventual consistency for autonomy.
elements.named_in: What do you mean by 'Event-Driven'? - Fowler (martinfowler.com, 2017)

elements.name: API Composition
elements.what: A composer queries multiple services and joins their results in memory to answer a query that spans service-owned databases.
elements.problem: Queries crossing database-per-service boundaries need an answer without shared storage; simple but limited by in-memory join cost.
elements.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - API Composition - Richardson (living)

elements.name: Database per Service
elements.what: Each service exclusively owns its persistent data; other services access it only through the service's API.
elements.problem: Shared databases couple services at the schema level; private data enables independent evolution and technology choice, at the cost of cross-service queries/transactions.
elements.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - Database per Service - Richardson (living)

elements.name: Service Discovery
elements.what: A registry tracks live service-instance locations; clients or routers resolve logical service names against it at request time.
elements.problem: In elastic deployments instance addresses churn constantly; static configuration cannot route to dynamically placed instances.
elements.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - Service Registry / Client-side Discovery - Richardson (living)

elements.name: Distributed Tracing
elements.what: Every external request gets a trace id propagated through all service hops; per-hop spans are collected centrally to reconstruct the end-to-end path.
elements.problem: In a request that crosses many services, latency and failure localization are impossible from per-service logs alone.
elements.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - Distributed Tracing - Richardson (living); canonical system: Dapper - Sigelman et al. (Google, 2010)
elements.borderline: Observability infrastructure sits near operations; kept as it is a named cross-cutting system structure and the bridge endpoint for the design realm's correlation-id mechanisms.

elements.name: Health Endpoint Monitoring
elements.what: Services expose endpoints reporting their own health; external agents (monitors, orchestrators, load balancers) probe them to route or restart.
elements.problem: A process can be up yet unable to serve; standardized self-reported checks let infrastructure detect and react to partial failure.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Health Endpoint Monitoring - Azure Architecture Center (living)

elements.name: Polyglot Persistence
elements.what: A system deliberately uses multiple storage technologies, matching each data-management need to the store best suited for it.
elements.problem: One database type fits neither graph, document, relational, and cache workloads all at once; trades operational diversity for per-need fit.
elements.named_in: PolyglotPersistence - Fowler (bliki, 2011)

elements.name: Reporting Database
elements.what: A separate database, fed from the operational store, structured and indexed for reporting/analytics queries.
elements.problem: Reporting workloads distort and degrade the operational schema and its performance; offloading isolates both.
elements.named_in: ReportingDatabase - Fowler (bliki, 2004)

elements.name: Enterprise Service Bus
elements.what: A shared messaging backbone providing routing, transformation, protocol bridging, and orchestration between enterprise applications.
elements.problem: Point-to-point integration among N systems explodes to N^2 adapters; a mediating bus centralizes translation and routing (and becomes its own coupling point).
elements.named_in: Enterprise Service Bus - Chappell (2004)

elements.name: Materialized View (architecture pattern)
elements.what: Precomputed, query-shaped copies of data are generated and refreshed from source-of-truth stores to serve reads the source format handles poorly.
elements.problem: Query shapes that would need expensive joins/scans against the write-optimized store; trades staleness and refresh machinery for read performance.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Materialized View - Azure Architecture Center (living)
elements.borderline: The database-internal materialized view is a storage mechanism; kept here in its architecture-pattern sense (cross-store derived read models), per parked data-tier decision.

elements.name: Primary-Replica Replication
elements.what: One node accepts all writes and streams its change log to replicas, which serve reads and can be promoted on failure.
elements.problem: Read scale-out and failover for a single-writer dataset while keeping a simple consistency story on the write path.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

elements.name: Multi-Leader Replication
elements.what: Several nodes accept writes concurrently and asynchronously replicate to each other, requiring conflict resolution.
elements.problem: Accept writes in multiple datacenters or offline clients; trades single-writer simplicity for write availability plus conflict handling.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

elements.name: Leaderless Replication
elements.what: Clients (or coordinators) write to and read from multiple replicas directly, using read/write quorums, read repair, and hinted handoff instead of a leader.
elements.problem: High write availability under node failure and partition without failover machinery; trades strict ordering for quorum-tunable consistency.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

elements.name: Sharding
elements.what: A dataset is split by key across nodes (range or hash partitioning) so each shard is stored and served independently, with rebalancing and request routing.
elements.problem: Data or write volume exceeds one node; partitioning scales linearly but introduces routing, rebalancing, hot spots, and cross-shard operations.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

elements.name: Leader Election
elements.what: Cooperating instances select exactly one of themselves as coordinator for a role, and re-elect when the leader fails.
elements.problem: Some actions must be done by exactly one instance in a fleet of equals; election plus failure detection avoids both split-brain and a fixed single point of failure.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Leader Election - Azure Architecture Center (living)

elements.name: Two-Phase Commit
elements.what: A coordinator drives distributed atomic commit: participants first vote prepared, then all commit or all abort on the coordinator's decision.
elements.problem: Atomicity across multiple resource managers; the price is blocking on coordinator failure and latency of two round trips.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017); original treatment: Gray, Notes on Data Base Operating Systems (1978)

elements.name: Distributed Snapshot
elements.what: Marker messages flow through a distributed system's channels so each node records a mutually consistent cut of global state without stopping the world.
elements.problem: Consistent global checkpoints for recovery/exactly-once processing when no node can observe the whole system at one instant.
elements.named_in: Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems - Chandy & Lamport (ACM TOCS, 1985)

elements.name: Distributed Commit Log
elements.what: A partitioned, replicated append-only log serves as the system's ordering and integration backbone; producers append, consumers replay at their own pace.
elements.problem: Give many decoupled systems one durable, ordered, replayable record of what happened, unifying messaging, replication, and stream processing.
elements.named_in: The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction - Kreps (LinkedIn Engineering, 2013)

elements.name: Bulkhead (deployment isolation)
elements.what: System capacity (instances, pools, clusters) is partitioned into isolated compartments per client, workload, or function so one compartment's failure cannot exhaust the rest.
elements.problem: Shared capacity lets one misbehaving consumer or dependency sink the whole system; compartments cap the blast radius.
elements.named_in: Release It! - Nygard (2007)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm's bulkhead is the in-process resource-partitioning mechanism (pools, queues); this is the deployment/topology sense.

elements.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
elements.what: A queue is placed between producers and a service so bursts are absorbed by the queue and the service consumes at its sustainable rate.
elements.problem: Intermittent heavy load overwhelms downstream services provisioned for average demand; the buffer converts bursts into throughput-bounded work.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Queue-Based Load Leveling - Azure Architecture Center (living)

elements.name: Throttling (service admission control)
elements.what: A service enforces consumption limits per tenant/client and degrades or rejects excess requests to protect its SLA under load.
elements.problem: Autoscaling has limits and lag; explicit admission control keeps the system functional when demand exceeds capacity.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Throttling - Azure Architecture Center (living)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm carries throttle/rate-limiter mechanisms (token bucket, sliding window); this is the system-boundary policy structure.

elements.name: Deployment Stamps
elements.what: The full solution is replicated as identical scale-unit deployments (stamps), each hosting a subset of tenants/load, with routing in front.
elements.problem: Scale beyond a single deployment's limits and isolate tenants by adding units instead of growing one deployment.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Deployment Stamps - Azure Architecture Center (living)

elements.name: Geodes
elements.what: Identical active-active deployments distributed across geographic regions, each able to serve any user, backed by globally replicated data.
elements.problem: Serve a global user base with low regional latency and region-loss tolerance, instead of active-passive DR.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Geodes - Azure Architecture Center (living)
elements.borderline: Name currency is largely Azure-specific; the structure (geo-distributed active-active units) is real and bridgeable, so kept with the caveat.

elements.name: Competing Consumers (system topology)
elements.what: Multiple independently deployed consumer instances pull from one shared message channel, so load spreads and any instance's failure is absorbed by the rest.
elements.problem: Scale-out and resilience of asynchronous message processing across nodes without a dispatcher knowing the consumers.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm's competing-consumers is the in-process worker-pool-on-queue mechanism; this entry is the multi-instance topology sense (per charter judgment call).

elements.name: Client Session State
elements.what: Session state is held on the client (cookies, hidden fields, client storage) and sent with each request; servers stay stateless.
elements.problem: Server statelessness for scale-out and failover; trades bandwidth, security exposure, and size limits on session data.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Server Session State
elements.what: Session state is kept in the application server's memory (possibly serialized or replicated) between requests.
elements.problem: Simplest handling of rich session data; costs sticky routing or replication and complicates failover and scale-out.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Database Session State
elements.what: Session state is committed to shared persistent storage between requests, keyed by session, readable by any server instance.
elements.problem: Session survival across server failures and free request routing; costs a database round-trip per request and cleanup of dead sessions.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

rejected.name: Big Ball of Mud
rejected.why: Anti-pattern (Foote & Yoder 1997), excluded by mission rule; noted per charter instruction.

rejected.name: Onion Architecture
rejected.why: Palermo (2008) names the same concentric dependency-rule structure Martin generalizes; kept as aka on clean-architecture per charter fold decision. Hexagonal kept separate (ports/adapters is a distinct named structure with its own naming source and mechanism emphasis).

rejected.name: Compensating Transaction (Azure)
rejected.why: The compensating action is the saga's constituent mechanism, not a separate topology; folded as aka.

rejected.name: Gateway Aggregation / Gateway Routing / Gateway Offloading (Azure)
rejected.why: Three facets of the single gateway role; folded as aka to avoid triple-counting one structure.

rejected.name: Unidirectional Data Flow (umbrella)
rejected.why: Family umbrella over Flux/Elm/MVI - a catch-all node is worthless by mission rule; the concrete named members (Flux, Elm Architecture) are cataloged and the umbrella name is annotated as aka on Flux.

rejected.name: Health Check API (Richardson)
rejected.why: Same structure as Azure's Health Endpoint Monitoring; Richardson's name folded as aka, Azure entry kept as canonical because the naming source is corpus-citable (azurepatterns).

rejected.name: Event Notification (Fowler 2017)
rejected.why: Fowler's event-notification is the plain pub-sub interaction (thin events, callback for state); the distinct mechanism he separates out - event-carried state transfer - is cataloged as its own element.

rejected.name: Three-Phase Commit
rejected.why: Skeen's non-blocking variant of 2PC - algorithm-variant granularity (algorithmics zoo); 2PC carries the architectural slot.

rejected.name: Broker
rejected.why: POSA1 scout's territory (Broker is a POSA1 architectural pattern); not carried here to avoid duplicate ids - merge step should verify it landed.

rejected.name: REST
rejected.why: Charter assigns REST to the shaw-garlan-tmd scout; skipped here per instruction.

rejected.name: Blackboard
rejected.why: POSA1 scout carries it per charter.

rejected.name: Layered Architecture / Pipes-and-Filters
rejected.why: Canonical Shaw-Garlan/POSA1 styles belonging to those scouts; my n-tier entry covers only the physical-tier enterprise variant.

rejected.name: Presentation-Abstraction-Control (PAC)
rejected.why: POSA1 scout may carry per charter; not duplicated here.

rejected.name: Microkernel / Plug-in Architecture
rejected.why: POSA1 pattern (also a Richards & Ford style); left to the POSA1 scout - merge step should verify it landed.

rejected.name: Message Broker / Message Bus / integration styles (File Transfer, Shared Database, RPC, Messaging)
